lesson.title: When Non-Boolean Values Act Like True or False
lesson.summary: Python lets any value, not just True and False, be tested in a boolean context by following truthiness rules that treat certain values as falsy and everything else as truthy.
lesson.body:
So far, every boolean expression in this chapter has been built from things that are already boolean: literals, comparisons, and the results of and, or, and not. Python actually allows any value at all, of any type, to be used where a boolean is expected, such as directly inside an if statement's condition. To make that possible, Python defines rules for which values count as equivalent to False, called falsy values, and treats every other value as equivalent to True, called truthy.

The falsy values are worth memorizing because they are consistent across the language: the number 0, the float 0.0, the empty string "", the empty list [], the empty tuple (), the empty dictionary {}, and the special value None, along with False itself. Every other value Python can produce, a nonzero number, a nonempty string, a list with at least one element, is truthy. This is a design choice with a clear underlying logic: the values Python treats as falsy are, in a real sense, all representations of nothing or empty, while a truthy value represents that something is there.

Trace this example:

items = []
if items:
    print("Cart has items")
else:
    print("Cart is empty")

Python does not compare items to anything explicitly here; it evaluates items directly in the if statement's condition. Since items is an empty list, and an empty list is falsy, the condition behaves as if it were False, so the else branch runs, printing "Cart is empty". If even one item had been added to the list beforehand, items would be truthy, and the if branch would run instead.

This connects directly back to short circuit evaluation from the previous section. and and or do not actually convert their results into a plain True or False; they return whichever original operand determined the outcome. "" or "default" evaluates to "default", not to True, because the empty string is falsy, so or moves on to evaluate and return its right side. This truthiness system is also why experienced Python code often writes if name: instead of the more verbose if name != "":. Both work, but the first relies on truthiness directly and is considered more idiomatic.

A subtlety worth flagging directly: the string "0" is truthy, even though it visually represents zero, because truthiness for strings depends only on whether the string is empty, not on what characters it contains. bool("0") evaluates to True, while bool(0), the actual integer, evaluates to False. This distinction trips up programs that read numeric input from a text file or a web form, since that input arrives as a string; checking if user_input: only confirms that some text was entered, not that the text represents a nonzero number, and the two checks are not interchangeable.

Numeric values follow the same all except zero rule regardless of sign: both 5 and -5 are truthy, since neither one equals zero, and only the value 0 itself, whether written as an int or as a float, counts as falsy.
